content_pack.topic_name: Motion in One Dimension: Displacement, Velocity, and Acceleration

body_json.hook_question: Between a habal-habal (motorcycle taxi) and a jeepney leaving Barangay Poblacion at the same time along the same route, which one really arrives first — and does 'faster' always mean the same thing as 'covers more distance'?
body_json.scenario: Two vehicle icons travel a straight local route. The jeepney takes a longer, winding path along its usual stops; the habal-habal takes a shorter, more direct path.
body_json.prediction_prompt: Which vehicle do you think arrives first?

prediction_options.label: They arrive at the same time

teacher_answer_key.answer: No. Speed is a scalar quantity (distance divided by time). A vehicle taking a longer, winding route can still cover more distance at a higher speed, but its displacement — the straight-line distance from start to finish — may end up equal to or less than a vehicle that travels a shorter, more direct path. This is the core distinction the lesson builds toward: distance/speed describe how much ground was covered, displacement/velocity describe the net change in position.
teacher_answer_key.teaching_note: There is no single 'correct' predicted winner — the point of this stage is surfacing the distance-vs-displacement misconception before instruction, not testing it. Accept any prediction; the value is in the reasoning students give (see prediction_options' reasoning_options) and in returning to this same clip once vectors are formally defined in Explain.

body_json.instructions: Mark an 8–10 meter path (hallway or classroom aisle). In groups of 4–5, walk the path at a steady pace, then walk forward and back to the start. Measure and record the distance covered, the displacement, and the time taken for each trial using a tape measure and stopwatch.

teacher_answer_key.teaching_note: Trial 3 is the pedagogically important row: constant, non-zero average speed (2.00 m/s — the student never stopped moving) alongside zero average velocity (they returned to the start). This is the single clearest classroom demonstration of the distance/displacement distinction and is worth calling out explicitly rather than letting it pass as just another data row.

lesson_stages.display_title: Graph Visualizer: Slope, Area, and the Kinematic Equations

definitions.note: Total path length covered, regardless of direction.
Straight-line change in position, with direction.
Displacement per unit time, with direction.
Rate of change of velocity per unit time.

derivation_steps: Start from the definition of acceleration: a = (v - v0) / t
Multiply both sides by t: a*t = v - v0
Add v0 to both sides: v0 + a*t = v
Average velocity over constant acceleration: v_avg = (v0 + v) / 2
Displacement: d = v_avg * t = ((v0 + v) / 2) * t
Substitute v = v0 + a*t: d = ((v0 + v0 + a*t) / 2) * t
Substitute into eq2: d = v0*(v - v0)/a + 0.5*a*((v - v0)/a)^2
Simplify and solve for v^2: v^2 = v0^2 + 2*a*d
Average velocity for uniformly accelerated motion: v_avg = (v0 + v) / 2
Displacement equals average velocity times time: d = v_avg * t

graph_reading_summary: Displacement-time (d-t) graph: slope = delta_d / delta_t = velocity (v)
Velocity-time (v-t) graph: slope = delta_v / delta_t = acceleration (a)
Velocity-time (v-t) graph: area under curve = displacement (delta_x)
teacher_answer_key.teaching_note: Full step-by-step derivations for all four kinematic equations are already provided per-equation in this stage's kinematic_equations.derivation_steps field — this summary is a quick-glance version for the teacher dashboard, not a replacement for the full derivations.

body_json.intro: Use the kinematic equations to determine whether a rider can still catch the last boat trip at the port, or how quickly a tricycle must slow down to stop safely at a hump.

body_json.instructions: Read each question carefully and select the best answer. Use the principles of distance, displacement, speed, velocity, acceleration, and the kinematic equations discussed in class to solve the problems.

quiz_items.prompt: A tricycle travels 3 km east then returns 3 km west back to its starting point. What is its total displacement?
quiz_items.explanation: Displacement is the straight-line change in position. Since the tricycle returns to its starting point, the net displacement is 0 km, even though it traveled 6 km of total distance.
quiz_items.teacher_formula: delta_x = x_final - x_initial = 0 km - 0 km = 0 km

quiz_items.prompt: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
quiz_items.explanation: Velocity has both magnitude and direction, making it a vector quantity. Distance, speed, and time are scalar quantities.
quiz_items.teacher_formula: Velocity has magnitude AND direction -> vector. Distance, speed, time are scalars.

quiz_items.prompt: A jeepney covers 500 m in 25 s at constant speed. Compute its average velocity.
quiz_items.explanation: Average velocity = displacement / time = 500 m / 25 s = 20 m/s.

quiz_items.prompt: On a velocity-time graph, what does the slope of the line represent?
quiz_items.explanation: The slope of a velocity-time graph represents the rate of change of velocity, which is acceleration.
quiz_items.teacher_formula: slope of v-t graph = delta_v / delta_t = acceleration

quiz_items.prompt: On a displacement-time graph, what does the slope represent at any point?
quiz_items.explanation: The slope of a displacement-time graph at any point represents the instantaneous velocity.
quiz_items.teacher_formula: slope of d-t graph = delta_d / delta_t = velocity

quiz_items.prompt: A motorcycle accelerates uniformly from rest to 20 m/s in 4 s. Determine its acceleration.
Using v = v0 + at, find the final velocity of a car that starts at 10 m/s and accelerates at 2 m/s² for 5 s.
What physical quantity is equal to the area under a velocity-time graph?
quiz_items.explanation: The area under a velocity-time graph represents the displacement over that time interval.
quiz_items.teacher_formula: area under v-t curve = velocity x time = displacement

quiz_items.prompt: Which pair correctly distinguishes a scalar quantity from a vector quantity?
quiz_items.explanation: Distance is a scalar quantity (magnitude only), while displacement is a vector quantity (magnitude and direction).
quiz_items.teacher_formula: Distance = scalar (no direction); Displacement = vector (has direction)

quiz_items.prompt: A cyclist travels 150 m north in 30 s, then rests for the next 10 s. What is the cyclist's average velocity for the whole 40 s trip?
quiz_items.explanation: Average velocity = total displacement / total time = 150 m / 40 s = 3.75 m/s north. The resting period counts toward total time even though no additional displacement occurs.
quiz_items.teacher_formula: v_avg = delta_x_total / t_total = 150 m / (30+10) s = 3.75 m/s north

mission_levels.title: Catch the Last Trip
mission_levels.scenario_text: A habal-habit is traveling from one barangay to a school. The rider needs to know their average velocity to determine if they can catch a scheduled boat trip at the port before it departs.

mission_levels.title: Stop at the Hump
mission_levels.scenario_text: A tricycle approaching an intersection with a road hump is traveling at 15 m/s and must come to a complete stop in 5 s to cross safely. Determine the required acceleration (deceleration).

teacher_solution.given: v0 = 15 m/s, v = 0 m/s, t = 5 s
